newsitem.title: INDIA: New Kashmir leader returns to hero's welcome.
newsitem.headline: New Kashmir leader returns to hero's welcome.

text.p: Thousands of joyful Kashmiris turned out to greet their new leader Farooq Abdullah, when he arrived on Saturday in Srinagar, summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, after a landslide poll victory.
Abdullah's moderate National Conference party won 57 of the 87 assembly seats in India's northern Jammu and Kashmir state in the first local polls since a separatist revolt broke out in 1990.
Asked how he felt to be back in power after six years in the political wilderness, Abdullah, tall and silver-haired, clenched his fists. He raised his arms above his head and smiled.
"I feel like a tiger out of the woods," he told Reuters.
Abdullah was chief minister in 1990 when New Delhi dismissed the state government, saying it was soft on separatism.
Abdullah said he would do his best to reconcile the separatists, even though they have refused an offer, early this week, to enter into talks.
"No doors are closed," Abdullah said. "I do not close my doors. Even if they close their doors, I will break their doors and windows and open the way for negotiation."

Dozens of party workers broke through the police and security cordons to shower Abdullah with rose and marigold petals as he emerged from Srinagar airport. They garlanded him with flowers and strings of 100-rupee ($2.82) notes.
Police said about 8,000 people gathered to greet Abdullah, who wore a traditional long white cotton tunic and pyjamas.
"A new day has dawned in Kashmir," said Sadiq Ali, a diminutive white-haired deputy of Abdullah's party from the Zadibal constituency, five kms (three miles) north of Srinagar.
Busloads of people lined Abdullah's route from the airport. "Jiye, Jiye Farooq Jiye," ("Long live Farooq Abdullah") they chanted as he passed by.
Apple-cheeked schoolgirls in pigtails lined up by the side of the road to clap their hands as the convoy sped by in a cloud of grey Kashmiri dust.
But the police and paramilitary trooopers positioned every 15 yards along the route brought a sobering note to the occasion.
Scattered shouts of "Freedom for Kashmir", as well as the ancient Moslem cry of "Allah-o-Akbar", occasionally rent the air.
Dozens of Kashmiri separatist groups fighting for freedom or closer ties to neighbouring Pakistan have already rejected Abdullah's government.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence in the last six years.
The National Conference members met in a conclave later on Saturday and formally elected Abdullah the leader of their legislative party, party sources said.
He is expected to be sworn in as chief minister next Tuesday.
Abdullah will form the state's first elected government in nearly a decade. New Delhi ruled Kashmir directly for six years.
Abdullah's party won on a promise of greater autonomy for the state, which includes Hindu-dominated Jammu, predominantly Moslem Kashmir and the Buddhist area of Ladakh.
On Saturday he announced plans to implement it within a year.
"Autonomy for the three regions of the state, we shall do in one year," Abdullah said, speaking to reporters.
India's constitution gives the state control over all matters except foreign relations, defence and communications. Since 1952, the federal government has gradually claimed some of the power.
The separatists have rejected Abdullah's government, after boycotting the polls, as a "mockery of Kashmiri aspirations".
